newsitem.title: USA: FBI expert says O.J. Simpson hair was on knit hat.
newsitem.headline: FBI expert says O.J. Simpson hair was on knit hat.

text.p: A knit hat found at the scene where O.J Simpson's ex-wife and her friend were murdered contained hairs that matched those of the former football star, an expert witness testified on Tuesday at Simpson's civil trial.

Douglas Deedrick, head of the FBI's hair and fiber laboratory in Washington, said that 12 head hairs taken from the hat bore the same characteristics as hairs found on victim Ronald Goldman's shirt and both sets matched Simpson's.

Simpson, who was found not guilty by a criminal trial jury in October 1995, was not in court on Tuesday for the dramatic testimony. He was in another courtroom 50 miles (80 km) away in suburban Orange County fighting a legal battle to win custody of the two young children he had with his slain ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson.
He was being sued in civil court by the victims' families seeking damages for the wrongful deaths of their loved ones.
In key testimony for the plaintiffs, Deedrick was asked by attorney Edward Medvene if microscopic comparisons of different hairs could identify a single person.
"It is not an absolute identification," Deedrick said, but added that in 19 years of studying hairs, he had never seen two with the same characteristics.
He said Negroid hair found on Goldman's shirt and in the hat bore the same characteristics as a control sample from Simpson.
"Either O.J. Simpson wore the hat, or someone else who has the same microscopic characteristics," Deedrick said.

Asked if he had compared the Negroid hairs on the hat and shirt to other samples from police officers and others who had visited the crime scene after the June 1994 killings, Deedrick said: "There were no hairs from any of these people. Only one matched. It was O.J. Simpson."
Earlier, the trial took on a dramatic tone as Simpson attorney Robert Baker clashed with forensic pathologist Werner Spitz, an expert witness for the plaintiffs, during cross- examination.
At one point, Baker tried to argue that scratches and cuts on Simpson's hand could not have been made by Goldman during his fatal struggle with a knife-wielding assailant.

Asked if he had concluded that Goldman's fingernails could not have caused "gouge" wounds to Simpson, Spitz replied, "No, Mr. Goldman had short fingernails. I do too." He explained that even short nails could cause such injury.
At this point, Baker approached Spitz, holding out his forearm: "Gouge me!" he said.
"Do you want me to scoop tissue out?" asked Spitz in his heavy German accent.
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki interjected, setting off laughter in the court when he said: "Mr. Baker, I'm not going to have any gouging of flesh."

Spitz, a retired county medical examiner in Michigan, then rolled up his own shirtsleeve to demonstrate. "When you are fighting for your life and dig in deep without concern if you are hurting, you pull back the fingernail and it becomes longer," said Spitz.

Asked specifically by Baker if Goldman could have caused the cuts on Simpson's hand, Spitz replied: "I am not able to look at fingernail marks and say who made them. I can say Mr. Goldman could have made them."
He acknowledged that no analysis had ever been made of Goldman's fingernails. Of Nicole Brown Simpson's nails, he said: I understand she had fake fingernails. They were glued on."
He said that there was a substance that could have been blood under her fingernails.
During cross-examination, Baker tried to get him to change his previous testimony that Nicole Brown Simpson died in about 15 seconds and that Goldman was left for dead after about one minute.
But the combative, white-haired pathologist stood his ground, often earning Baker's ire.
